episode.title: Part 1 — What They Built, and Who Got Named
episode.titleFull: ENIAC, Part 1 — What They Built, and Who Got Named
episode.subtitle: The machine, the press release, and the photographs judged unsuitable for publication
episode.description:
Credit for ENIAC was assigned four separate times, by four different mechanisms, over roughly thirty years: a press office in January 1946, an institution — in job titles and pay grades — for years afterward, a market in the 1950s, and a federal court in 1973. This series is about that machinery of assignment, not about naming a single inventor. Part 1 covers the first two documents. On January 17, 1946, Herman Goldstine sent the Army a batch of photographs of the machine and the people who ran it; the captions name them, by name and hometown, and describe them setting switches and plugging cables. Thirteen days later, the War Department's Bureau of Public Relations issued a release naming three men — Eckert, Mauchly, Goldstine — as primarily responsible for the difficult technical phases of the work. It went to every newsroom in the country. The photographs were judged unsuitable for publication.

In between: why the machine got built (the Army's firing-table backlog), who built it (Eckert and Mauchly, and the hundred-plus women employed as human computers before there was a machine at all), how it worked reliably despite eighteen thousand vacuum tubes (digital pulse regeneration, not better tubes), and what it actually ran first — a classified hydrogen-bomb feasibility calculation, not an artillery trajectory. The episode corrects roughly fifteen widely repeated claims about ENIAC along the way and says, at each point, exactly where the documented record runs out. It never calls ENIAC "the first computer," and explains why that word describes a definition, not a fact.

episode.voice_note: NOT Nick's cloned voice. The project's locked rule specifies 'Nick 2' via ElevenLabs; ELEVENLABS_API_KEY and VOICE_ID were unset, the pipeline was stopped, Nick was asked, and he directed the use of an OpenAI stock voice and chose 'onyx' from three samples. Explicit and chosen, not a silent fallback. See project.json -> phases.voice.deviation. If this ships as the published version rather than a draft, decide whether to re-render in Nick 2 first — the script is unchanged by the voice choice, so a re-render costs synthesis time only.

loudness.target: -16 LUFS integrated, true peak <= -1.0 dBTP (project standard for mono spoken word)
loudness.note: Two-pass ffmpeg loudnorm, measured off the final encode rather than the intermediate. The pre-encode true-peak target was set to -1.5 dBTP because targeting -1.0 exactly produced post-encode overshoot above spec — a known lossy-codec reconstruction artefact.
